title: Is the blood in your veins blue?
hook: Anyone who has had blood drawn knows the answer.
summary: Never: human blood is always red. Veins look blue because of how light travels through skin.

cardBlocks.text: Human blood is never blue. After picking up oxygen in the lungs, it is bright red as it heads into the arteries; on the way back to the heart through the veins, having given up its oxygen, it is dark red. Blood drawn into a sealed vacuum tube, with no contact with air, still comes out dark red. And a vein seen directly, inside the body, isn’t blue either.

So why do veins look blue through the skin? It comes down to how light travels through skin. Compared with red light, blue light doesn’t penetrate skin as well and is more likely to be scattered back to your eye. Over a vein that lies a little deeper, the light that returns looks bluish. How the brain processes colour plays a part too.
Blood is always red; veins look blue because of how light travels through skin and how the brain reads colour.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Depth matters. A vein very close to the surface can actually look reddish, while deeper veins look blue, because blue light can’t reach as deep as red light.
An old question, studied with physics

In 1996, a team led by Alwin Kienle published a study in the journal Applied Optics called “Why do veins appear blue? A new look at an old question”. The answer lies in the optics of the skin and in how we perceive colour, not in the colour of the blood.
All animals with backbones, humans included, have red blood. But some animals, such as lobsters, crabs, octopuses, squid, mussels and clams, really do have blue blood.

heroMedia.alt: Diagram of light entering skin: red light goes deeper and is absorbed by the vein, while blue light scatters near the surface and returns to the eye, so the deep vein looks bluish.

claims.text: Human blood is always red, never blue.

support.excerpt: Our blood is not blue. It is always red.

claims.text: Blood is bright red after picking up oxygen in the lungs and heading into the arteries; returning through the veins without that oxygen, it is dark red.

support.excerpt: When the hemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs, the blood is a bright cherry red as it heads into the arteries
On its return trip to the heart through the veins, the oxygen-depleted blood is dark red or maroon, because the hemoglobin is no longer bound to oxygen.

claims.text: Blood drawn into a vacuum tube, without contact with air, is still dark red.

support.excerpt: Even when it's deoxygenated. Even in the absence of oxygen in a vacuum.
when you get blood drawn at your doctor's office, they use a vacutainer, which is essentially a vacuum in a tube.
I drew hundreds of samples of venous blood. Almost all samples were dark red.

claims.text: A vein seen directly inside the body is not blue.

support.excerpt: when you poke around inside a human being and see a vein or artery in its naked glory, it isn't blue.

claims.text: Compared with red light, blue light penetrates skin less and is more likely to be scattered back to the eye.

support.excerpt: blue light, compared to red light 1) doesn't penetrate the skin as well, 2) is absorbed by the blood more, and 3) is more likely to be scattered and make it back to your eye.

claims.text: Veins very close to the surface can look reddish, while deeper veins look blue because blue light can’t penetrate as deeply as red.

support.excerpt: if a vein is close to the surface of the skin, most of the blue light will be absorbed, and even though red light doesn't reflect as much, the red light:blue light ratio is high enough to make the vein appear red.
But the blue light's inability to penetrate as deeply as red light makes the veins appear blue.

claims.text: Veins look blue because of the skin’s light-scattering properties and how the brain processes colour, not because of the blood, which is dark red.

support.excerpt: The factors that contribute to this alteration of color perception are related to the light-scattering properties of the skin and the processing of visual input by the visual cortex, rather than the actual colour of the venous blood which is dark red.
